what_its_for: Haloperidol lactate is used to treat mental health conditions such as schizophrenia and other disorders that cause confused thinking, hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), or agitation. It may also be used to control severe behavioral problems and reduce uncontrolled body movements or sounds (such as in Tourette syndrome).
how_to_take: Haloperidol lactate is a liquid that is usually given as a shot (injection) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital setting. If you are taking it at home in liquid form by mouth, use the measuring dropper that comes with your medication to measure the exact dose. You can mix it with water, juice, or another beverage to make it easier to swallow. Take it at the same time each day. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your condition, age, and how well you respond to treatment. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor may start you on a low dose and slowly increase it. Follow your doctor's instructions exactly. The right dose is different for each person.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store haloperidol lactate liquid at room temperature, away from light and heat. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Do not freeze the liquid, as freezing can damage the medication. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting too hot or overheated, as this medicine can make it harder for your body to control its temperature. Avoid standing up too quickly, as this medicine can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, making you feel dizzy or faint. Tell your doctor before taking any other medications, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: stiff muscles, high fever, confusion, or sweating (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); uncontrolled muscle movements in your face, tongue, or body (tardive dyskinesia); irregular or fast heartbeat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; seizures; severe dizziness or fainting; unusual changes in mood or behavior; signs of infection such as fever or chills; or if you feel worse instead of better.
when_it_works: Some people may notice an improvement in agitation or behavior within a few hours of the first dose, especially with an injection. For ongoing mental health conditions like schizophrenia, it may take several days to a few weeks before you notice the full benefit of this medicine. Be patient and keep taking it as prescribed, even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults: This medicine should be used with extra caution in elderly patients, especially those with dementia, as it may increase the risk of serious side effects including falls, strokes, or death. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who took this medicine near the end of pregnancy may have withdrawal symptoms. Breastfeeding: This medicine can pass into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine may be used in children for certain conditions, but only under close supervision by a doctor.
